course.name: Data Preparation at Scale: Contracts, Synthetic Data and Privacy

los.description: Design shared data contracts, a pseudonymous linkage key and a breaking-change policy for a feed with several producers, given three producers whose extracts disagree on schema, codes and units
Implement an incremental, idempotent preparation pipeline over partitioned columnar tables with quality gates, given 30 million synthetic rows on a laptop
Evaluate a synthetic dataset for fidelity, analytical utility and disclosure risk, given two generators fitted to related patient and encounter tables
Compute differentially private statistics under a budget shared across repeated releases, given twelve monthly statistics
Select a privacy-enhancing method for each data request by comparing protection, utility and cost, given four requests, from an internal analyst to an external university
Decide whether to release a dataset and on what conditions, and defend the decision, given the university request and the measured results

questions.prompt: All three producers' weight columns pass "a number between 1 and 500". What do you do before pooling them?
options: Pool them: the rule passed for every producer
Divide Rawdah's values by 2.2 in the study notebook
Compare the distributions by producer and confirm the unit with each producer
Drop weight from the study
questions.explanation: A unit difference passes type and range checks. The distribution shows it, the producer confirms it, and the factor goes into the contract for every consumer.
misconceptions: Trusts a range wide enough to hold pounds and kilograms alike
Fixes a symptom in one consumer's code and tells nobody
Throws away good data because one producer differs

questions.prompt: Ufuq confirms its creatinine is in mg/dL. Where should the factor 88.42 be written?
options: In the contract, as a unit clause for Ufuq's creatinine
In the preparation pipeline's cleaning step
In Ufuq's hospital system, by changing its unit
In the study's analysis notebook, with a comment
questions.explanation: In the contract the producer and every consumer read the same rule, and changing it becomes a versioned change with notice.
misconceptions: Hides the rule in one pipeline where other consumers never see it
Pushes a consumer's need onto the producer's own system
Turns a fixed rule into a habit that each analyst may forget

questions.prompt: Ufuq offers to send SHA-256 of each national identifier instead of the identifier. What do you answer?
options: Accept: hashed data is anonymous
Accept if they remove spaces first
Ask for the plain identifier and hash it centrally
Ask for a keyed hash of the normalised identifier, with a project key the consortium does not hold
questions.explanation: A plain hash of a ten-digit identifier is reversed in hours on one core. A secret key held elsewhere makes the pseudonym impossible to recompute for the consortium.
misconceptions: Treats a reversible hash as anonymisation
Improves only the format while the space stays small enough to enumerate
Moves the identifier, not the risk: the consortium would then hold identities

questions.prompt: Rawdah plans to rename weight_lb to weight and send kilograms. Its engineer calls it a minor clean-up. How do you classify it?
options: Minor: one column, same data
Breaking: a rename and a unit change; major version, notice and a parallel run
Additive: the new unit is better
Whatever Rawdah decides: it owns the data
questions.explanation: Every consumer that reads weight_lb breaks, and any that converts pounds now gets wrong numbers. Both are breaking under the policy.
misconceptions: Judges a change by its size in the code, not by its effect on consumers
Assumes the unit change is good news, but any consumer converting pounds now divides kilograms
Lets the producer's own judgement replace the agreed policy

questions.prompt: Rawdah tells you that from next month its weight column will hold kilograms, under the same name. What do you do first?
options: Classify it under the policy as a breaking unit change: new major version, notice, a parallel run
Thank them and remove the unit clause from the contract the same day
Add an if-statement on the date in the study's pipeline
Nothing: the range rule will catch any problem
questions.explanation: Same name, new unit is the change no schema diff shows. The policy treats it as breaking so that every consumer moves together.
misconceptions: Assumes a change towards the standard unit cannot hurt, when every consumer that converts pounds now divides kilograms
Moves the fix into one consumer's code where the other consumers never see it
Trusts a range rule that pounds and kilograms both pass

questions.prompt: Your lazy query on the lake is fast but its peak memory is the same as the eager script's. Which change most likely helps?
options: Rewrite the lake as one unpartitioned Parquet file, so fewer files are opened
Run it on more CPU cores
Collect the labs table first, then filter it
Read the plan: put the month and test filters on the scan and select only needed columns
questions.explanation: Memory follows what is read. If the plan shows a full projection or no selection on the scan, the query reads everything; pushing filters and columns down is what saves memory.
misconceptions: Removes the partitions that let the scan skip whole files, so even more is read
Adds threads to a problem of bytes read
Caches the very data that should never have been loaded

questions.prompt: Sidra's delivery on day 5 corrects results first delivered on day 2. Which load leaves exactly one row per result, holding the corrected value?
options: Append each day's file
Merge each day's file on encounter, test and round
Overwrite each day's partition
Append, then drop rows that are identical in every column
questions.explanation: Only matching on the business key finds the earlier row a correction refers to, wherever it was loaded.
misconceptions: Repeats every row each time the day is loaded
Replaces day 5's partition but leaves the originals in day 2's
Removes duplicates by every column, so the corrected and original rows both stay

questions.prompt: A release from last March must be reproduced. The run log names the table but not the version, and the table is vacuumed weekly with seven days' retention. What is true?
options: Read the table as of last March's timestamp
It cannot be rebuilt exactly from the table; only a kept snapshot of the release would prove it
Rebuild from today's table: corrections only improve it
Restore the table to March and rerun
questions.explanation: Time travel needs both the log entry and the data files; vacuum removed the files. Record versions and keep release snapshots.
misconceptions: Assumes time travel works without the files the old version needs
Today's data includes every correction since March
Restoring needs the same files that vacuum removed

questions.prompt: Rawdah's September laboratory partition fails its gate. The study's monthly report is due today. What does the pipeline do?
options: Stop the whole load until Rawdah re-sends
Publish it with a warning in the log
Publish the 35 partitions that passed, quarantine Rawdah's September, and flag September as two producers
Divide the partition's values by 88.42 and publish
questions.explanation: Gating per partition keeps a bad delivery from blocking good ones, and the flag keeps the figure honest about what it contains.
misconceptions: Stops good data from two producers and eleven months because of one partition
Publishes known bad values into the study
Repairs a producer's data downstream without the producer confirming the cause

questions.prompt: Sidra corrects 15 creatinine results three days after sending them. Your daily load overwrites the delivery day's partition. What does the curated table hold afterwards?
options: The corrected values only
Both the original and the corrected results: 15 duplicate keys
Only the latest day, everything else overwritten
An error: the keys collide
questions.explanation: Partition overwrite makes a re-run safe but files the correction under the day it arrived. Only a merge on the business key replaces what it corrects: Lab 2.2 counted 15 duplicate keys before the merge and 0 after.
misconceptions: Assumes overwrite by day reaches rows that belong to an earlier day
Confuses a predicate overwrite with a full table rewrite
Expects the table to enforce a key it was never given

questions.prompt: The ministry asks for the number of readmissions per region and month, published on a public dashboard. Which option fits?
options: A synthetic file the ministry counts itself
A de-identified extract
A query service on the real data, with small counts protected before publication
The exact counts from the real data, as they are
questions.explanation: Counts must come from the real data; but a public count of 1 or 2 can identify someone, so outputs are protected too. Day 4 session 2 does this with a privacy budget.
misconceptions: Gives counts that are model draws, wrong most in the small cells a dashboard shows
Hands patient-level rows to someone who needs only totals
Treats publication as private because no rows leave

questions.prompt: A colleague fits one generator to patients and another to encounters, then assigns each synthetic encounter to a random synthetic patient. What breaks first?
options: Who comes back: stays per patient no longer depend on the patient's conditions
Referential integrity: encounters with no patient
The marginal distribution of each column
The overall readmission rate
questions.explanation: Random parents keep every column and every link, but heart-failure patients get 2.10 stays instead of 3.06, and some patients get none.
misconceptions: Integrity can hold perfectly while the relation is lost
Each table on its own is generated as before
Assumes the outcome's average changes when only its link to patients is lost

questions.prompt: A generator's report shows every column's distribution within 2% of the real one. The university asks whether its readmission model will work. What do you answer?
options: Yes: the distributions match
Train on synthetic and test on the real training data
Not known yet: train on synthetic, test on a real holdout, and compare the study's estimates
No synthetic data can support a model
questions.explanation: The independent baseline matches every marginal and still shrinks the heart-failure effect from 2.07 to 1.16.
misconceptions: Takes column-by-column similarity as evidence for relationships
Tests on data the generator learnt from, which rewards copying
Dismisses a measurable question

questions.prompt: A membership-inference test on a synthetic encounter table gives an AUC of 0.51; on the patient table, 0.88. What do you conclude?
options: The release is safe on average
Patient attributes are coarse, so the 0.88 does not matter
The encounter test failed and should be re-run
The patient table leaks its training patients; the release fails until it is fixed
questions.explanation: A release passes only if every table passes: an attacker uses the weakest one, and the tables link through the identifier.
misconceptions: Averages away the table that leaks
Assumes coarse attributes cannot identify anyone
Reads an AUC near 0.5 as a failure of the attack rather than as protection

questions.prompt: A new generator gives a TSTR AUC of 0.706, equal to the model trained on real data, and a membership AUC of 0.97 on encounters. What do you report?
options: The best generator so far: release it
Acceptable on average across the two measures
The attack is unreliable when utility is this high
It copies its training encounters: it fails, and its perfect utility is part of the evidence
questions.explanation: The vendor's file showed exactly this pattern: zero fidelity gap, the real AUC, and members found with certainty.
misconceptions: Reads perfect utility as success without the attack that contradicts it
Averages a leaking table with a safe one
Blames the attack for the result it was built to detect

questions.prompt: An extract of patients with all their stays shows 4% of patients unique on sex, year of birth and region. What do you tell the release board?
options: The risk is low: 4%
The 4% ignores the stays: with two known stays nearly every patient with two is unique
Release only the first two stays of each patient and the risk is solved
The study identifiers are pseudonyms, so uniqueness does not matter
questions.explanation: An adversary's knowledge of stays makes the sequence a quasi-identifier: 96.6% unique at two known stays.
misconceptions: Reports the single-table estimate for a longitudinal release
Assumes removing stays always lowers risk
Treats pseudonyms as protection against someone who knows the person

questions.prompt: The ministry's dashboard recomputes every past month each night with fresh noise at ε = 1/12. The ledger is charged only once per month. What happens?
options: Privacy improves: the noise keeps changing
Nothing: each month is still released at ε = 1/12
Anyone who averages the nightly values recovers the true counts; the real spend grows every night
The dashboard fails when the budget runs out
questions.explanation: Every noisy copy is a release. A year of copies brought January within two patients of the truth.
misconceptions: Thinks fresh noise each night adds protection
Assumes the budget is a property of the query rather than of the releases
Confuses an accounting error with a software error

questions.prompt: Three hospital groups compute a pooled readmission count by secure aggregation and publish it. Which statement is true?
options: The aggregator never sees a site's count, but two sites together can compute the third's from the published total
No one can learn anything about any site's count
The published total is approximate because of the masks
The aggregator must be trusted with every site's count
questions.explanation: The masks cancel exactly: the output is the true total, and subtraction by those who know the other inputs reveals the last one.
misconceptions: Extends protection of the inputs to the published output
Confuses masking with noise
Assumes the protocol needs a trusted party to see values

questions.prompt: The synthetic pair passes every attack. The university's request still lacks its academic authority's written approval. What does the board decide?
options: Approve: the file is safe, so the approval is a formality
Reject the request permanently
Conditional approval: nothing moves until the request comes through the institution with written approval, on the form
Send a de-identified extract instead, which needs no approval
questions.explanation: An academic applicant applies through the institution with written approval of its academic authority; the method decides what is released once the request is complete.
misconceptions: Lets measured safety replace a requirement the rules place on the applicant
Ends the request when its gaps can be fixed
Sends real records to a requester who has not met the rules

questions.prompt: Sidra's creatinine median is 89.9 and Ufuq's is 1.00. Both columns are numeric and complete. What is the most likely explanation, and what follows?
options: Ufuq's patients have healthier kidneys; pool the values as they are
Ufuq reports mg/dL; confirm with Ufuq and write the factor 88.42 into the contract
One of the columns is corrupt; drop creatinine from the study
The medians differ by chance; compare means instead
questions.explanation: A ratio near a known unit factor points to a unit difference; the producer confirms it and the contract states the conversion for every consumer.
misconceptions: Reads a unit difference as a clinical difference
Discards a usable field instead of asking the producer
Treats an 88-fold difference as sampling noise

questions.prompt: Rawdah's diagnosis codes look like i50.9 and Ufuq's like I509. A colleague joins all three extracts to a diagnosis lookup on the raw code. What happens?
options: The join fails with an error, so the problem is found at once
Only codes in the lookup's exact format match, so most Ufuq and Rawdah rows drop out silently
The database ignores case and dots, so all rows match
Every row matches, some to the wrong diagnosis
questions.explanation: An inner join on codes that were not normalised drops what does not match exactly, without any error; the contract's format rule prevents it.
misconceptions: Expects a silent mismatch to raise an error
Assumes joins normalise text
Confuses missed matches with wrong matches

questions.prompt: Ufuq's latest delivery passes every column rule, but its newest admission is nine days before the delivery date. The contract allows two. What should the gate do?
options: Block the delivery and ask Ufuq to send a complete extract again
Accept it: every row is valid
Accept it and fill the missing days with the average of earlier days
Accept it and note the gap in the study's limitations
questions.explanation: Freshness is a contract clause: a delivery that stops early biases pooled rates, so the gate blocks it and the producer sends it again.
misconceptions: Treats completeness of a period as a property of single rows
Invents data to hide a gap
Lets a known bias into the pooled rate when a new delivery is possible

questions.prompt: Which clause belongs in the shared contract rather than in one consumer's pipeline code?
options: The colour scheme of the study's dashboard
The study's model settings
Ufuq's mapping of discharge codes 1 to 4 onto HOME, TRANSFER, DIED and LAMA
The name of the notebook that reads the feed
questions.explanation: Code maps define what the producer's values mean; written in the contract, every consumer applies the same meaning and a change to it is versioned.
misconceptions: Mixes a consumer's presentation choice with the feed's meaning
Puts an analysis choice into the producers' agreement
Confuses a consumer's file with the contract

questions.prompt: Producers will send HMAC-SHA-256 of the normalised national identifier. Who should hold the key?
options: The consortium's analysts, so they can check matches
Nobody: generate it once and delete it
Each producer its own key
A linkage unit outside the analysis team, which gives the producers one key for this project
questions.explanation: The producers need one shared key to produce matching pseudonyms; keeping it away from the analysts keeps the pseudonyms irreversible for them, and a key per project prevents joins across projects.
misconceptions: Gives the people who see the data the means to re-identify it
Producers need the same key to compute matching pseudonyms
Different keys give different pseudonyms, so nothing links

questions.prompt: Adding a second linkage key on name, birth date and sex raised recall from 0.993 to 1.000 and lowered precision from 1.000 to 0.988. What should you report?
options: Only the recall: the study needs every readmission
Both numbers with counts: 14 pairs recovered, 24 strangers merged, and a proposed rule to filter them
Only precision: wrong links are unacceptable
Neither: the truth file is synthetic, so the numbers mean nothing
questions.explanation: Linkage makes two errors that bias the study in different directions; the decision needs both, as counts as well as rates.
misconceptions: Hides the merged histories the second key created
Hides the readmissions the first key misses
Rejects measurement because the data is synthetic, when the planted truth is exactly what makes it measurable

questions.prompt: Ufuq replaces column Creatinine_mgdl by Creatinine, whose median is 89.3 where the old one was 1.00. How does the policy classify it?
options: Additive: a new column appeared
No change: the same measurement under a clearer name
Breaking: a renamed column and a unit change; a new major version
Breaking only if the data protection officer objects
questions.explanation: The values show the same measurement in a new unit: a rename and a unit change, both breaking, so the contract moves to a new major version.
misconceptions: Reads the schema diff and not the values
Misses the unit change hidden by the rename
Confuses the approvers with the classification

questions.prompt: Why is a new value in a closed code set (Ufuq's discharge code 5) treated as breaking?
options: The study's mapping does not know it, so those rows become null or drop out
Any change to a producer's system is breaking
New codes always mean worse data quality
It is not: new values are always additive
questions.explanation: A consumer with a closed list cannot place the new code, so its rows silently leave the analysis; the producer must announce it.
misconceptions: Over-classifies changes that consumers do not notice
Judges the value instead of its effect on consumers
Ignores that consumers with closed lists lose the rows

questions.prompt: A lazy query over the partitioned lake filters on month = '2025-09' and test_code = 'CREAT' and selects two columns. What does the plan let the scan skip?
options: Nothing: lazy only delays the same work
Only the columns it does not select
Every partition file whose month is not 2025-09, and every column the query does not need
Every row group, because the test filter is applied after loading
questions.explanation: Hive partition values prune whole files and projection pushdown reads only the needed columns; the plan shows both on the scan.
misconceptions: Confuses deferring work with reducing it
Forgets partition pruning by the folder names
Assumes filters run after the scan instead of inside it

questions.prompt: On 30 million rows an eager script peaks at 2.7 GB and the streaming lazy query at 112 MB, with the same result. What explains most of the difference?
options: The lazy query reads only the needed partitions and columns and aggregates batch by batch
Polars compresses data in memory better than pandas
The eager script has a bug that copies the data
The streaming engine uses the disk instead of memory for everything
questions.explanation: The eager script loads every row and column before filtering; the lazy plan reads less and the streaming engine never holds the whole result of the scan.
misconceptions: Credits the library instead of the amount of data read
Assumes a defect when the design reads everything by intent
Confuses batching with spilling all data to disk

questions.prompt: A nightly load appends the day's file. It crashed after writing and the scheduler re-ran it. What do you find in the morning?
options: An error in the log and an empty day
The day's rows twice, and no error anywhere
The day's rows once, because the table rejects duplicates
A corrupted table that cannot be read
questions.explanation: An append is not idempotent: the second run adds the same rows again, and nothing in the file or the table complains.
misconceptions: Expects a re-run to fail loudly
Assumes a table enforces a key it was never given
Confuses a duplicated write with a broken one

questions.prompt: Which test proves that a daily load is idempotent?
options: The load finishes without errors twice in a row
Row counts after one load and after two loads are within 1%
The table has no null values after the second load
A fingerprint of the table after loading every day once equals the fingerprint after loading every day twice
questions.explanation: Identical output when a day is re-run is shown by equal content fingerprints that ignore row order and file layout.
misconceptions: Takes absence of errors as proof of identical content
Accepts a tolerance where identity is required
Checks a quality property instead of sameness

questions.prompt: The December figures sent to the board were built from the curated table. Since then, corrections were merged. The run log recorded version 1. How do you reproduce the board's figures?
options: Rebuild from today's table and subtract the corrections
Read the table at version 1, rebuild the analysis and compare its fingerprint with the recorded one
Restore last month's backup of the whole lake
Re-run the analysis today: the figures are close enough
questions.explanation: Time travel to the recorded version rebuilds exactly what was read, and the fingerprint proves the rebuild is identical.
misconceptions: Reverses changes by hand instead of reading the old version
Uses a coarse backup when the table keeps its own versions
Accepts different numbers as a reproduction

questions.prompt: Why can vacuuming a table with a short retention break reproducibility?
options: It deletes the data files that older versions still need
It deletes the commit log, so versions lose their numbers
It rewrites every file, changing all fingerprints
It never does: vacuum only removes temporary files
questions.explanation: Vacuum removes files no longer referenced by the current version; time travel to an older version then fails for lack of its files.
misconceptions: Confuses removing data files with removing the log
Assumes vacuum rewrites current data
Ignores that old versions' files are exactly what vacuum removes

questions.prompt: One of 36 laboratory partitions fails its range gate with 16.7% invalid results. Why gate per partition rather than per load?
options: Partitions are faster to check than the whole table
A per-load gate cannot compute shares
One bad delivery is quarantined while the other partitions are published
Per-partition gates need no rules in the contract
questions.explanation: Blocking per partition stops only the failing producer and month; the rest of the data reaches the study, with the gap flagged.
misconceptions: Picks a speed reason for a decision about blocking
Assumes the rule cannot be computed on a whole load
Thinks the gate replaces the contract's rules

questions.prompt: A monthly figure dips in September. With OpenLineage run events for every job, how do you find the cause?
options: Read the pipeline code line by line
Walk the events backwards from the figure's dataset to the runs that wrote it and the partitions they read, then inspect September's partitions
Ask each producer whether they changed anything
Re-run the whole pipeline and see if the dip remains
questions.explanation: Lineage events record inputs and outputs per run, so the upstream walk narrows the dip to a handful of partitions whose data can be checked.
misconceptions: Ignores the events that record what each run actually read
Starts with people instead of the evidence that narrows the question
Repeats the problem without locating it

questions.prompt: A pharmacovigilance team needs the actual records of patients in a rare group (obstetric stays with chronic kidney disease). Which option fits?
options: A synthetic file of the whole study
A de-identified extract of that group under an agreement, with minimum columns
Monthly counts from a query service
A synthetic file restricted to that group
questions.explanation: Only real records serve case review; a synthetic file loses or invents rare cells. The extract is still personal data, so it needs an agreement and controls.
misconceptions: Expects a generator to reproduce the members of a rare group
Gives totals to a team that must review cases
Assumes conditioning on a rare group makes its records real

questions.prompt: In a synthetic file, cells with fewer than 10 real encounters are off by 153% on average and cells with 50 or more by 10%. What follows for a request for exact small counts?
options: Use the synthetic file but round the counts
Generate a larger synthetic file to reduce the error
Use the synthetic file: 10% is acceptable
Answer from the real data through a query service, protecting small counts before publication
questions.explanation: Synthetic counts are draws from a model and are worst exactly where small counts matter; exact counts come from the real data, with output protection.
misconceptions: Treats a model's draw as a count with rounding error
Expects more draws from the same model to recover exact rare counts
Reads the large-cell error as if it applied to small cells

questions.prompt: A university wants patient-level rows to develop a readmission model. Which plan states its residual risk honestly?
options: Send a synthetic file: synthetic data carries no risk
Send the pseudonymised table: no names are in it
A synthetic file for development, released only after per-table attacks pass, with the final model fitted on real data by the consortium
Refuse: no option is safe
questions.explanation: The synthetic file serves development; its privacy is shown by attacks and its utility by the gap to the real model, which is why the final fit stays on real data.
misconceptions: Takes the word synthetic as a privacy guarantee
Forgets that pseudonymised data stays personal data
Ignores options whose risk can be measured and controlled

questions.prompt: Encounters are generated with one model and patients with another, and each encounter gets a random patient. What is lost?
options: How the number and kind of stays depend on the patient
Referential integrity between the two tables
The distribution of each encounter column
Nothing, if both models are good
questions.explanation: The child count and the children's values depend on the parent; random parents keep every column and lose the relation (stays per heart-failure patient fell from 3.06 to 2.10).
misconceptions: Thinks random assignment creates orphans, when every encounter still has a patient
Expects the separate models to change their own marginals
Assumes good tables make a good relation

questions.prompt: In a conditional-tree generator, each value is copied from a random real row in the same leaf, and every leaf holds at least 25 real rows. What does raising the leaf size do?
options: Keeps relationships better and copies less
Has no effect: the leaf only affects speed
Increases copying, because larger leaves hold more real rows
Copies less and blurs relationships the analysis needs
questions.explanation: A larger leaf draws each value from a broader context: less like any one person, and less faithful to the relations between columns.
misconceptions: Assumes privacy and utility move together
Misses that the leaf is the context a value is drawn from
Confuses more rows to draw from with closer copies

questions.prompt: A generator matches every column's distribution within 2%. Trained on its data, the readmission model scores AUC 0.665 on the real holdout; trained on real data, 0.706. What do you report?
options: Utility is high: the marginals match
The file loses relationships the model relies on: a gap of 0.041 to the real model
The test is wrong: AUC should be measured on the synthetic data
Utility cannot be measured without the generator's code
questions.explanation: Train-on-synthetic, test-on-real measures fitness for the study; the gap to the real model is the evidence, whatever the fidelity scores say.
misconceptions: Takes column fidelity as fitness for the analysis
Scores the model on the data it was trained on
Thinks utility depends on the method rather than on the output

questions.prompt: On real data the readmission risk ratio for heart failure is 2.07 (1.84 to 2.33). On a synthetic file it is 1.16 (0.96 to 1.41). What does this mean for the study?
options: The synthetic file is fine: both show heart failure raises risk
The synthetic file is more private, so its estimate is better
A study run on it would report no clear effect: the file is not fit for this analysis
Average the two estimates
questions.explanation: Utility is judged on the analysis's own estimate; this file shrinks the effect towards 1 and would change the study's conclusion.
misconceptions: Ignores that one interval includes no effect
Confuses privacy with correctness of an estimate
Combines a biased estimate with an unbiased one

questions.prompt: A vendor's synthetic file gives a membership-inference AUC of 1.00 on encounters and 0.90 on patients. What do you tell the release board?
options: The file copies its training records: it fails, whatever it is called
The attack is broken: a synthetic file cannot score 1.00
It passes on average across tables
Exact twins in coarse tables explain it; accept the file
questions.explanation: Members are found with certainty: the file reproduces real stays under new identifiers. A release passes only if every table passes.
misconceptions: Trusts the label over the measurement
Averages away the weakest table an attacker would use
Forgets that chance matches affect non-members equally

questions.prompt: Why compare synthetic records with a holdout the generator never saw, rather than count exact matches with the training data?
options: Exact matches are too slow to compute
The holdout is larger, so the test is more precise
Exact matches are always zero in good synthetic data
Chance matches happen for anyone; only members being closer than non-members shows memorisation
questions.explanation: On coarse attributes about a fifth of never-seen patients have exact twins; the leak is the difference between members and non-members.
misconceptions: Gives a speed reason for a question of evidence
Misremembers the role of the holdout
Expects no chance matches on coarse attributes

questions.prompt: An extract shows 4% of patients unique on sex, year of birth and region. With two known stays (month and diagnosis group) added, 97% of the patients who have two stays are unique. Which number describes the extract's risk?
options: 4%: the stays are not identifiers
97%, for an adversary who knows two stays: the sequence of stays is a quasi-identifier
The average of the two
Neither: pseudonymised data cannot be re-identified
questions.explanation: Risk depends on what an adversary may know; for longitudinal records, stays a relative or colleague knows single out almost everyone with them.
misconceptions: Treats only demographic columns as quasi-identifiers
Averages two answers to different questions
Forgets that pseudonymised data stays personal data

questions.prompt: Truncating each patient's history to two stays dropped 24% of stays and raised uniqueness at two known stays from 21% to 47%. Why did the risk rise?
options: Truncation adds new information to each record
The adversary knows more after truncation
Other patients' later stays were the crowd that matched a person's known stays; removing them left fewer candidates
It did not: the measurement must be wrong
questions.explanation: Uniqueness counts candidates who share what is known; removing stays from everyone removes candidates, so a lever must be measured, not assumed.
misconceptions: Assumes risk can only rise by adding data
Moves the change to the adversary instead of the data
Assumes a protective-sounding lever cannot backfire

questions.prompt: Monthly counts of readmitted stays are to be released with Laplace noise. One patient can have three readmitted stays in a month. What should be done first?
options: Bound each patient's contribution, for example by counting readmitted patients, and calibrate the noise to that bound
Use the same noise as for a count where each person adds one
Remove patients with more than one stay
Add noise only to months with such patients
questions.explanation: The noise scale is the contribution bound divided by ε; a statistic in which each patient moves each count by at most 1 keeps the guarantee for patients.
misconceptions: Ignores that a person can move the count by more than one
Changes the population instead of bounding the contribution
Reveals which months contain them

questions.prompt: A yearly budget of ε = 1 is split over twelve monthly counts with Laplace noise. What is the expected absolute error of one month, and how do you halve it?
options: 1 patient; halve it by rounding
12 patients; halve it by adding a second noisy release and averaging, at no charge
12 patients; halve it by publishing only the months with large counts
12 patients; halve it with twice the budget per month, or with half as many releases
questions.explanation: With bound 1 and ε = 1/12 per month the Laplace scale, and the expected absolute error, is 12; halving it needs twice the ε per release.
misconceptions: Confuses ε with the noise scale
Thinks averaged re-releases are free
Turns the choice of months into a disclosure

questions.prompt: A dashboard recomputes last month's count every night with fresh noise, but the ledger records only the first release. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: each copy has the same ε
Each copy is a release; averaging them recovers the true count, so the real spend grows nightly
The counts will drift upwards
The ledger will refuse after twelve nights
questions.explanation: Sequential composition adds up every release; store and serve the first noisy value, or charge every recomputation.
misconceptions: Treats the budget as a property of the query rather than of the releases
Expects bias from unbiased noise
Forgets that the ledger was never charged

questions.prompt: Three hospital groups pool a readmission count by secure aggregation and publish the exact total. Sidra and Ufuq compare notes. What can they learn?
options: Nothing: secure aggregation hides every input
Only an approximate value for Rawdah
Rawdah's exact count: the total minus their own
Each patient's record at Rawdah
questions.explanation: The masks cancel exactly; anyone who knows all inputs but one can subtract. Outputs need their own protection: minimum sites and cells, or noise.
misconceptions: Extends protection of inputs to the output
Confuses masks with noise
Overstates what an aggregate reveals

questions.prompt: In a pairwise-mask protocol, one site drops out after agreeing its masks. The others reveal the masks they shared with it so the sum can be recovered. What must the aggregator then refuse?
options: A late masked value from the dropped site
Any further values from the surviving sites
Publishing the recovered sum
Nothing: recovery has no consequence
questions.explanation: With its masks revealed, the dropped site's late value could be unmasked alone; the protocol refuses it once recovery starts.
misconceptions: Blocks the sites whose values are still protected
Treats recovery as a breach of the total
Misses that the dropped site's masks are now known

questions.prompt: A professor emails a request for all record-level columns, for a thesis, with institutional approval 'to follow'. The synthetic pair passes every attack. What does the release board decide?
options: Approve the synthetic pair now: it is safe
Send a de-identified extract, which needs no approval
Reject the request permanently
Conditional approval: resubmission through the institution with written approval, on the form, with the minimum necessary data
questions.explanation: The secondary-use rules require an academic applicant to apply through the institution with written approval and to ask for the minimum necessary; the method applies once the request is complete.
misconceptions: Lets measured safety replace requirements placed on the applicant
Thinks an extract escapes the rules for personal data
Ends a request whose gaps can be fixed

questions.prompt: Which line belongs in a release decision record as a residual risk?
options: 'Data will be handled responsibly'
'Membership AUC 0.55 on patients and 0.51 on encounters, under the board's threshold of 0.60; the file remains derived from personal data'
'Synthetic data carries no risk'
'The risk is low'
questions.explanation: A residual risk states what was measured, against which threshold, and what remains; the board and the data protection officer can then check it.
misconceptions: Writes an intention that cannot be checked
Takes the label as the evidence
States a conclusion without the measurement
